case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND, REVISE

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.
